expectedText:
BACKGROUND CHECK ADVERSE ACTION NOTICE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the two-step notice process the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) requires before an employer takes an adverse employment action based on a consumer report, together with the individualized-assessment and notice process California's Fair Chance Act requires when an employer bases a decision on an applicant's or employee's conviction history. It states facts about what federal and California law require of Acme, Inc. in that situation. It is not itself a pre-adverse-action notice, an individualized assessment, a final adverse-action notice, or a decision, and it does not tell Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee what to do about any particular applicant, employee, or background-check result.

THE FEDERAL TWO-STEP PROCESS, STEP ONE: THE PRE-ADVERSE-ACTION NOTICE
Before Acme, Inc. takes an adverse employment action against Jordan Lee based in whole or in part on a consumer report, federal law requires two things to happen first: Jordan Lee must receive a copy of the report itself, and a written description of consumer rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act — both provided before the adverse action is taken, not after. This step is commonly called the pre-adverse-action notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in subparagraph (B), in using a consumer report for employment purposes, before taking any adverse action based in whole or in part on the report, the person intending to take such adverse action shall provide to the consumer to whom the report relates— (i) a copy of the report; and (ii) a description in writing of the rights of the consumer under this subchapter, as prescribed by the Bureau under section 1681g(c)(3)"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, pre-adverse-action requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681b)
  Known gap: The statute doesn't set a minimum number of days that must pass between providing this pre-adverse-action notice and taking the final adverse action — it requires only that the report copy and rights description be provided before the adverse action is taken, without specifying how long after that a final decision may follow. A narrower exception, not addressed in this document, lets certain transportation-industry applicants who apply by mail, phone, computer, or similar means receive a different, after-the-fact notice instead.

THE FEDERAL TWO-STEP PROCESS, STEP TWO: THE FINAL ADVERSE-ACTION NOTICE
Once Acme, Inc. actually takes an adverse action against Jordan Lee based in whole or in part on information in a consumer report, a second, separate notice requirement applies under a different part of the same federal law. Acme, Inc. must provide notice of the adverse action itself, the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency that furnished the report, a statement that the agency did not make the decision and cannot explain the specific reasons for it, and notice of Jordan Lee's right to obtain a free copy of the report and to dispute its accuracy or completeness with that agency.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Duties of users taking adverse actions on basis of information contained in consumer reports If any person takes any adverse action with respect to any consumer that is based in whole or in part on any information contained in a consumer report, the person shall— (1) provide oral, written, or electronic notice of the adverse action to the consumer;"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, final adverse-action notice (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681m)
  "(3) provide to the consumer orally, in writing, or electronically— (A) the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency (including a toll-free telephone number established by the agency if the agency compiles and maintains files on consumers on a nationwide basis) that furnished the report to the person; and (B) a statement that the consumer reporting agency did not make the decision to take the adverse action and is unable to provide the consumer the specific reasons why the adverse action was taken; and (4) provide to the consumer an oral, written, or electronic notice of the consumer’s right— (A) to obtain, under section 1681j of this title, a free copy of a consumer report on the consumer from the consumer reporting agency referred to in paragraph (3), which notice shall include an indication of the 60-day period under that section for obtaining such a copy; and (B) to dispute, under section 1681i of this title, with a consumer reporting agency the accuracy or completeness of any information in a consumer report furnished by the agency."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)(3)-(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, final adverse-action notice content (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681m)
  Known gap: This final notice may be given orally, in writing, or electronically — the statute doesn't require any particular format or a stand-alone document the way the earlier disclosure step does. Federal law also specifically forecloses states from adding their own separate requirements on these particular duties (see the relationship clause below), so this description states the federal floor without layering any state-law content on top of it here.

CALIFORNIA'S FAIR CHANCE ACT: INDIVIDUALIZED ASSESSMENT AND PRELIMINARY NOTICE
Separately, if Acme, Inc. is considering denying Jordan Lee a position solely or in part because of conviction history, California's Fair Chance Act requires an individualized assessment before any such denial — whether that conviction history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job, considering the nature and gravity of the offense or conduct, the time that has passed since the offense or conduct and completion of sentence, and the nature of the job held or sought. If Acme, Inc. reaches a preliminary decision to disqualify Jordan Lee on that basis, California law requires written notice of that preliminary decision before it becomes final — identifying the disqualifying conviction(s), including a copy of the conviction history report if any, and explaining Jordan Lee's right to respond and the deadline for doing so.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer that intends to deny an applicant a position of employment solely or in part because of the applicant’s conviction history shall make an individualized assessment of whether the applicant’s conviction history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job that justify denying the applicant the position. In making the assessment described in this paragraph, the employer shall consider all of the following: (i) The nature and gravity of the offense or conduct. (ii) The time that has passed since the offense or conduct and completion of the sentence. (iii) The nature of the job held or sought. (B) An employer may, but is not required to, commit the results of this individualized assessment to writing. (2) If the employer makes a preliminary decision that the applicant’s conviction history disqualifies the applicant from employment, the employer shall notify the applicant of this preliminary decision in writing. That notification may, but is not required to, justify or explain the employer’s reasoning for making the preliminary decision. The notification shall contain all of the following:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, individualized-assessment requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  "(A) Notice of the disqualifying conviction or convictions that are the basis for the preliminary decision to rescind the offer. (B) A copy of the conviction history report, if any. (C) An explanation of the applicant’s right to respond to the notice of the employer’s preliminary decision before that decision becomes final and the deadline by which to respond. The explanation shall inform the applicant that the response may include submission of evidence challenging the accuracy of the conviction history report that is the basis for rescinding the offer, evidence of rehabilitation or mitigating circumstances, or both."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, required content of the preliminary notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: This requirement applies to employers with five or more employees, subject to statutory exceptions (for example, certain positions where a background check is otherwise legally required) that this document doesn't catalog. This provision was previously codified at Labor Code § 432.9; the current text of the California codes, as published by the California Legislative Information website, places it at Government Code § 12952 — the Labor Code section itself is currently blank on that site.

CALIFORNIA'S FAIR CHANCE ACT: RESPONSE WINDOW AND FINAL NOTICE
After receiving the preliminary notice described above, Jordan Lee has at least five business days to respond before Acme, Inc. may make a final decision. If, within those five business days, Jordan Lee notifies Acme, Inc. in writing of a dispute about the accuracy of the conviction history report and states that specific steps are being taken to obtain supporting evidence, Jordan Lee gets five additional business days — ten business days in total — to respond. If Acme, Inc. then makes a final decision to deny employment solely or in part because of conviction history, California law requires written notice of that final denial, any existing procedure Acme, Inc. has for Jordan Lee to challenge the decision or request reconsideration, and notice of the right to file a complaint with California's Civil Rights Department.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The applicant shall have at least five business days to respond to the notice provided to the applicant under paragraph (2) before the employer may make a final decision. If, within the five business days, the applicant notifies the employer in writing that the applicant disputes the accuracy of the conviction history report that was the basis for the preliminary decision to rescind the offer and that the applicant is taking specific steps to obtain evidence supporting that assertion, then the applicant shall have five additional business days to respond to the notice."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, response window (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  "If an employer makes a final decision to deny an application solely or in part because of the applicant’s conviction history, the employer shall notify the applicant in writing of all the following: (A) The final denial or disqualification. The employer may, but is not required to, justify or explain the employer’s reasoning for making the final denial or disqualification. (B) Any existing procedure the employer has for the applicant to challenge the decision or request reconsideration. (C) The right to file a complaint with the department."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, required content of the final notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: Neither the preliminary nor the final notice is required to explain the employer's reasoning, though either may. This clause states the business-day figures set by the statute itself; it doesn't address separate notice-timing and mail-service presumptions (for example, how many days after mailing a notice counts as received) that appear in the Fair Chance Act's implementing regulations rather than in the statute, which this document did not independently verify against the regulatory text.

HOW THE FEDERAL AND CALIFORNIA PROCESSES RELATE
When Acme, Inc. uses a third-party consumer reporting agency to run a criminal-history background check on Jordan Lee, the federal process and the California process described above are separate legal requirements that can both apply to the same background check. Federal law's general rule is that it does not override state law on the collection, distribution, or use of consumer information, except to the extent a state law actually conflicts with a specific federal provision. California's Fair Chance Act separately states that its own remedies are in addition to, and not a substitute for, whatever other rights and remedies an applicant has under other law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) In general Except as provided in subsections (b) and (c), this subchapter does not annul, alter, affect, or exempt any person subject to the provisions of this subchapter from complying with the laws of any State with respect to the collection, distribution, or use of any information on consumers, or for the prevention or mitigation of identity theft, except to the extent that those laws are inconsistent with any provision of this subchapter, and then only to the extent of the inconsistency."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681t(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, general state-law savings clause (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681t)
  "(C) subsections (a) and (b) of section 1681m of this title, relating to the duties of a person who takes any adverse action with respect to a consumer;"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681t(b)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, specific preemption of state adverse-action-duty requirements (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681t)
  "(e) The remedies under this section shall be in addition to and not in derogation of all other rights and remedies that an applicant may have under any other law, including any local ordinance."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, cumulative-remedies clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: Federal law does carve out one specific, narrower exception to that general rule: no state may impose its own separate requirement or prohibition specifically regulating "the duties of a person who takes any adverse action" under Section 1681m(a)-(b) of the federal law — the final-notice step described above. Whether, or to what extent, that narrower federal carve-out affects any part of California's Fair Chance Act process is a question this document does not resolve; answering it would require a preemption analysis, which is a legal conclusion, not a fact this document states. This document did not locate, and could not check for, a published court decision analyzing that specific interaction — CourtListener returned a rate-limit error when queried for this document, so no case law is cited on this point.

Date: _______________

Acme, Inc. certifies that this information sheet was provided to Jordan Lee.

Company representative: _______________
